full_judgment:
2. The facts of the case, in short, are that the appellants as pre-emptors instituted Miscellaneous Pre-emption Case No.44 of 1997 under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 in the Court of Assistant Judge, Keranigonj, Dhaka stating, it alia, that the land covering 62 acres of CS Plot No.110 appertaining to CS Khatian No.36 originally belonged to Sheikh Karim Bepari and Sheikh Abdul Hamed Bepari. Sheikh Karim Bepari died leaving behind two sons named Abdul Aziz and Abdul Wahab. Thereafter, Abdul Aziz Bepari expired leaving behind three sons named Mohammad Hossen, Md. Mobarak Hossain (defendant No.2), Md. Habibullah (defendant No.3) and one daughter named Foyjunnessa. Mohammad Hossen passed away leaving behind the pre-emptors as his sons and two daughters, namely, Mst. Latifa. Begum and Mst. Shamsunnahar (opposite party Nos.4 and 5 of the application for preemption). The vendor (opposite party No.2 of the application for preemption) transferred the case land to the pre-emptee (opposite party No.1) by a kabala deed dated 16.06.1997. The pre-emptee is a stranger purchaser. The pre-emptor came to know about the impugned kabala deed on 12.11.1997 and then filed the application for pre-emption. 

 4. The Assistant Judge considering the materials on record dismissed the application for pre-emption holding that the pre-emptor did not make any statement whether he has got land more than statutory limit or not. 

 9. Mr. S. N. Goswami, learned Advocate, appearing for respondent No.1 made sub-missions in support of the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division and further submitted that the High Court Division rightly pointed out that the case of oral gift pleaded in the written objection by pre-emptee No.2 in favour of pre-emptee No.1 was acted upon long before the kabala dated 16.07.1997 and that oral gift was acted upon at any time after liberation of Bangladesh, so the kabala deed is nothing but a showing of transfer without transferring any interest. He further submitted that the High Court Division rightly pointed out that there having passed no consideration money as against the alleged transfer dated 16.07.1997 and as such, exhibit No.2 cannot be considered as a sale deed within the meaning of section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act. He further submitted that the High Court Division rightly found that the kabala deed dated 16.07.1997 being not a deed of transfer for any price and having transferred nothing the same cannot come within the mischief of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and consequently, no right of pre-emption is available. He further submitted that a kabala deed ipso facto did not give rise to the right of pre-emption to a co-sharer ten-ant unless any real transfer of ownership was made for a price paid or promised or part paid and part promised. He further submitted that the case land was transferred by oral gift by pre-emptee No.2 earlier who disposed in the case agreeing the text of oral gift and who admitted in his deposition that no money transaction was made for the sale deed dated 16.07.1997, but it was a showing off transfer and as such, the pre-emption case was not maintainable. 

 11. Admittedly, the applicant-appellant is the co-sharer in the suit jote. It appears from exhibit No.3 that the case kabala deed is registered instrument which has been registered on 16.07.1997 on completion of all formalities as has been provided in section 60 of the Registration Act. It further appears from the case kabala that the case land was sold for taka 1,00,000.00 and though there are five per-sons who put their signature as attesting witnesses in the saf-kabala deed, but one is from pre-emptor party. OPW2, the vendor in his examination-in-chief stated that Abeda took him to Court to make a hiba deed and that the deed was not read out to him. There was no similarity in between the statement of the vendor and the written objection of the defendants. The trial Court observed that the case kabala was a saf-kabala deed. The trial Court also observed that the defendant failed to produce any receipt, voucher and deed in favour of their development cost of taka 1,00,000.00. It appears that the case was not bad for defect of parties and was not barred by limitation. The trial Court held that it was a miscellaneous case for pre-emption under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. To file a cast under section 96, the applicant had to state in the application regarding limitation of his-property under section 90 of the said Act. In the instant suit, the applicant nowhere in the application stated anything in respect of his total property as has been acquired by him with a view to fulfill the requirement of section 90 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The trial Court dismissed the suit having not found necessary documents relating to the pre-emption case. 

 12. The appellate Court on hearing both the parties and perusing the records found that the applicants are the co-sharers in the suit land and the case is not bad for defect of parties and is not barred by limitation and that the case is not adverse to the section 90 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. On the contrary, since opposite party No.1 is a stranger in the case property and the alleged deed is a saf-kabala deed, so under the facts and circumstances of the case, the applicant is entitled to preempt the case property. Moreover, since opposite party No.1 expended taka 1,00,000.00 having filled earth, constructed houses, planted trees, raised boundary walls and it is proved by the four witnesses, so he is entitled to have expenses. The appellate Court directed the applicants to deposit taka 1,00,000.00 within 90(ninety) days in favour of opposite party No.-1 failing which the order will be stand vacated. 

 20. Thus, from the evidence of OPWs. 1-5, it appears that he made a consistent statement with other OPWs to the effect that case land was transferred much earlier by an oral gift than that of the deed under pre-emption and pre-emptee No.1 being the recipient of oral gift constructed her homestead long before the alleged execution and registration of the deed under pre-emption. Since nothing has been transferred by the deed under pre-emption, the application of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act in the instant case is not maintainable against the said deed. Having regard upon those discussion of oral gift, sale deed, section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1950 and section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, the High Court Division held that the impugned judgments and orders are although judgment of reversal, but those are nothing but per-verse one inasmuch as those were recorded without discussing and considering the material evidence on record and was recorded upon emotion. 

 ". . in course of cross-examination if it is possible to unveil any fact which supports the case of cross-examiner or an indication is revealed from the lips of the witness of if the witness makes statement inconsistent with the chief, the Court may infer an adverse pre-emption against the party for whom he has deposed in the case . . ." 

 24. This word of admission goes to show that before execution of such kabala, pre-emptee No.2 gifted out such land in favour of his foster daughter. From the aforesaid observation made in the impugned judgment, we have no other alternative but to hold that the learned trial Court and the learned Judge of the Single Bench of the High Court Division has arrived at a correct decision to the effect that the instant deed under pre-emption was created only to avoid further complication, if any, might have arisen after the death of pre-emptee No.2 and no land has been transferred through this impugned deed except the transfer made by the oral gift long before from the deed in question. The pre-emptee appeared before the Court during hearing this case. We have come to know that except this .05 acre land, she had no other land. It appears to us that the balance of convenience are very much preponderant in favour of this lame and helpless lady. It further appears to us that soon after liberation war, the land in question has been converted into non-agricultural land as it appears from the admission of both the parties. Whereas the pre-emptor by suppressing this fact brought the present petition under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 instead of presenting the application for pre-emption under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949 which is not at all maintainable.
